4894.idn: Tima (ISO 639-3: tms), part of the Katla language group (Katla, Julut, Tima); data: Nuba mountains of Sudan; main speaker Hamid Kafi Daldum (b. 1968) plus seven further named male speakers; recordings collected between 2007 and 2010 as part of a language documentation and dictionary project
4894.tone: Two-tone system H/L plus downstepped H (treated as an allotone, not a toneme, except in a few lexicalized items); LH and HL contours on long vowels or short vowel + sonorant coda; minimal pairs at the lexical and grammatical level (noun vs verb, pluractionality, telicity). Instrumental f0 data from three male speakers (2326/2519 tokens). Positional tendencies reported are tonal only: 'In polysyllabic words, contour tones are more likely to occur on the last syllable of a word. Polysyllabic words are also more likely to begin with a Low tone' (p. 534). A case-insensitive full-text search of the publication finds no 'stress' or 'accent' at all; the only hits are 'Cepstral Peak Prominence', the SFB 1252 'Prominence in language' project name, and 'a final (usually falling) intonation' for the pause units of the transcribed passage (p. 535). There is also a falling tone H͡L which occurs word-finally'): a two-tone system with word-final contour, lexically and grammatically contrastive, cross-word H spreading diagnosing prosodic phrasing, utterance-final lowering; 'Duration does not appear to be a factor marking topic or focus constructions' (2025 p. 52). Stress/accent: no first-hand statement in any opened text. Kaldhol p. 72 reports that Stevenson (1942/2009 p. 17) devoted one page to 'possible tone or stress and its relationship to intonation', observed that 'inherent tone plays little part in distinguishing words' and tentatively concluded Tira 'is not a tone language in the fullest sense of the term'; Watters 1993 (abstract) says Tira 'is tonal', has two underlying tones H and L and four surface tones, and that ch. 3 'suggests what the relationships between tone, length and loudness are'. Modern work (Watters, Kaldhol) treats Tira as a tone language; the Stevenson hedge is 1940s data, unresolved and not reachable first-hand.

4899.heavy: A final (pre-clitic-boundary) syllable attracts stress 'a) when it is followed by a continuant, and/or, b) when it is [+long]'. Per the Table of Distinctive Features on p. 87, the [cont] row reads p- t- k- q- ȼ- č- s+ š+ ř- l+ m- n- ʔ- h+ w+ y+, so [+cont] = s š l h w y; p t k q ȼ č ř m n ʔ are [-cont] (ř, 'attested only in Spanish loan words and in a few onomatopoetic words', is [-cont] and [-son] in Watters' table). A final syllable closed by a stop, affricate, nasal, trill or glottal stop therefore counts as light, as does a short open final. Vowel length is phonemic (i i: e e: a a: o o: u u:). Only the final syllable's weight matters; the penult's weight is not consulted.
4899.dflt: penult: 'A vowel is stressed when it is separated from the clitic boundary by a following syllable and the following syllable a) contains a short vowel and is closed by a noncontinuant, or, b) is an open syllable with a short vowel.'
4899.prule: One stressed syllable per word. In the verb (domain closed by the clitic boundary ≠): stress on the final syllable when its vowel is long and/or is followed by a continuant consonant (s š l h w y); otherwise, when the final syllable has a short vowel and is open or closed by a noncontinuant (stops, affricates, nasals, ʔ, ř), stress on the penult. Only the final syllable's weight is evaluated (final-if-heavy, else penult). For other parts of speech the source states there is 'no consistent placement of stress' and gives no rule.

4900.prule: Tone language (three level tones: High, Mid, Low) with no identified stress system. Marlett & Weathers 2018 §7 p. 23: 'It is not clear whether something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Meꞌphaa. However, there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed.' The prominence described is a root-internal weak+strong structure (in a disyllabic root the final syllable is strong and the first weak; affixation leaves it unchanged; monosyllabic minor-class words behave as weak syllables), diagnosed through lenition of voiced plosives in weak syllables (Tlacoapa example /bìjú/ [bìjú] ~ [βìjú] 'hawk', §3.2.1 p. 9) and through long vowels being confined to the strong syllable (§8.2 p. 25; §4 p. 19 notes penultimate lengthening as subphonemic and contrastive length only in the word-final syllable). No stress rule; no accent rule. The Tlacoapa-specific orthography paper (Marlett 2018) states only the three tones (alto, medio, bajo) and the root-final stop allophony, and never uses 'acento' except for the acute mark of high tone.
4900.srule: Not mentioned in Marlett & Weathers 2018 (§7 'Prominence' pp. 23-24, §6 pp. 22-23, §5.2 p. 22, §8.2 p. 25 read): the source describes a single strong (root-final) syllable per root and no secondary, rhythmic or alternating prominence.

4901.prule: No word-level stress placement rule is stated for Tlacolulita in any reachable source. The language is tonal (contrastive tone; low tone realized with breathy voice, /jòʃ/ [jo̤ʃ˨˩] 'avocado'; monosyllabic low-tone /cʲèt͡ʃ/ 'thorn'). Stress is nonetheless treated as real by the documenter: in her transcriptions the (usually monosyllabic) root carries the stress and TAM prefixes never do (PFV /biˈɾe/, POT /iˈɾe/ 'run out'; /biˈgaˀtʃ/; /biˈtʃɛ̀ʔ/), and she states for Zapotec generally that 'since PTZ times, the root-initial syllable has been the most prominent in the phonological word', with pre-tonic prefix syllables toneless, a pattern she says she has 'personally observed' in Tlacolulita. The only explicit Tlacolulita prominence statement is phrasal: in a noun phrase or compound the final (modifier) root is prominent and the first root is non-prominent, with the fortis/lenis contrast neutralized there (kʲaʰt 'tortilla' vs ˌkʲaðeˈnaʔk 'yesterday's tortilla', ˌkʲaðenaˈlasˑ 'thin tortilla').
4901.srule: Word-level secondary stress: not mentioned in Beam de Azcona 2018 (Sonora paper, §§2-5), Beam de Azcona 2018 (COLOV VIII slides), Beam de Azcona 2023 (JHL preprint §2.1, §5) or Beam de Azcona 2023 (COLOV IX slides); Tlacolulita roots are mostly monosyllabic and prefixes pre-tonic. Only at noun-phrase/compound level: the first root is non-prominent (fortis/lenis neutralized) and is transcribed with a secondary-stress mark, the final root with the primary mark (kʲaʰt 'tortilla' ~ ˌkʲaðeˈnaʔk 'tortilla de ayer', ˌkʲaðenaˈlasˑ 'tortilla delgada') -- a transcription, not a discussed rule.

4903.prule: No stress rule is stated for Tlazoyaltepec Mixtec by any reachable source. The only statement whose scope formally includes it is Josserand's (1983:180) definition of the Mixtec couplet as 'composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two', seen second-hand: Carroll 2015:86 frames it as a generalization 'across Mixtec varieties' whose 'all varieties' implication he then qualifies with a named survey-town counterexample (Yoloxochitl, final stress); Penner 2019:91-92 reads the same page as a Proto-Mixtec claim. Tlazoyaltepec is one of Josserand's 122 survey towns (code Tlaz) but no Tlazoyaltepec data or statement appears in any opened text. If the catalog admits a family-level proxy, the proxy is couplet-initial (root/stem-anchored) stress, a set by morphology-type rule; it is not admitted here.

4906.dq: The following rules are concerned with the placement of accent in words. Such rules must account for the fact that a word will only have one accent mark in the terminal string (unless there is no inherent accent in any of the constituent forms). [1971, p. 47] ... This is the rule for zeroing all remaining innate accents within a word but the last one. [p. 50] Harrison 1975 p. 15, section 2.11: 'E…
4906.dloc: Harrison 1971: p. 47 (introduction to the accent rules) and p. 50 (Rule 29); Harrison 1975: section 2.11, p. 15
4906.prule: Accent is assigned per morpheme, not per word. Every accent-bearing formative (verb stem, noun stem, adverb, verbal suffix, particle) has an inherent accent on its own penultimate syllable; a monosyllabic formative's accent lands on the syllable before it (#o´ken# > #ó-ken#) or on itself when nothing precedes (#´ʔaŋ-a# > #ʔáŋ-a#). The nominal marker -a, D, past-tense words and other subjunctives carry no inherent accent; postpositions carry only a weak accent. Within the phonological word (#...# or #...//) all inherent accents but the last are zeroed (Rule 29), so each word surfaces with one accent, on the penult of its last accent-bearing morpheme. That is the word penult in verb + accented-suffix strings (o-apo-póta, o-apo-pam=tar-áme) and in monosyllabic stem + -a (ʔáŋ-a), but the word antepenult in disyllabic noun stem + -a (cáwar-a, ce-ráʔɨr-a; 1975 p. 41: 'O acento cai na penúltima sílaba de todo tema nominal') and further left when an accent-stripped postposition follows (ʔáŋ-a-pɨpe). Position is thus set by which morphemes carry inherent accent, not by word syllable count or weight.
4906.srule: Secondary accent is placed regressively on every other syllable counting leftward from the (single) word accent; VʔV counts as one syllable for the count. Example ɨwoʔoetɨmakɨŋáŋawa 'soap' with primary on ŋá and secondaries on ɨ, e, ma. Harrison treats it as an automatic phonetic rule and does not formalize it; nothing is said about the syllables after the primary.

4908.tone: Cotel 1907 p. XI: 'Ils ont trois intonations, le ton élevé, le ton moyen et le ton bas', shown on a musical staff with Kān'ga 'épaule' / 'bouteille' / 'esclave' — tone is presented as distinct from and additional to the 'accent tonique'. Tisserant 1930 p. 23: 'La langue banda est chantée... chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre... On distingue trois tons principaux' (haut, moyen, bas); pp. 23-24: 'En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots' — an intensity accent alongside tone, with no position stated. Tucker & Bryan 1966 §2: three tone levels H/M/L in the Banda group; 'stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length', with a tendency to extra shortness of the penultimate syllable in Ngbaka, Gbaya and Banda (Hackett's Togbo forms yavóró, abòrò, àgbòlò). So the lect is tonal with a reported stress-like accent on top; the coded rule is the accent position Cotel states.

4914.heavy: A short vowel counts as one mora and long vowel as two moras for the placement of stress. In Takic, syllable-final consonants also figure in the mora count, unlike the situation reported for Southern Paiute where the gemination or prenasalization of a consonant has no effect on stress placement (Sapir 1949:50-51).... A short vowel before another vowel does not count as a mora (and is often written as glide in the source materials)
4914.dflt: Second syllable (the syllable containing the second mora when the first syllable is light CV), e.g. hohuunar 'bears', honaar 'badger', a$aawt 'eagle'.
4914.prule: Primary stress falls on the syllable containing the second mora counted from the left edge of the phonological word, prefixes and reduplicative syllables included: a long vowel counts two moras and a coda consonant one, so an initial CVV or CVC syllable is stressed (huunar 'bear', paahonar 'great bear', aawverot), otherwise the second syllable (hohuunar 'bears', honaar 'badger', a$aawt 'eagle'); a short vowel before another vowel is non-moraic; enclitics are normally outside the count but may take stress after a short root.
